concept: PD autonomic dysfunction: orthostatic hypotension, constipation, bladder

claims.text: Mirabegron is not free of autonomic safety considerations: the urogenital review lists worsening hypertension and urinary retention among potential adverse effects, and PaDoMi reported an acute urinary-retention case. (medium confidence)

The cited review describes screening for orthostatic hypotension with supine blood pressure and heart rate followed by measurements after 3 minutes standing, and defines it as a systolic fall ≥20 mmHg and/or diastolic fall ≥10 mmHg; it also mentions a longer standing challenge when delayed hypotension is suspected. (low confidence)

The 2020 review recommends slow position changes, avoiding heat and large carbohydrate-rich meals, and stepwise nonpharmacological treatment; water and salt supplementation require caution in heart, kidney or liver failure. (low confidence)

NICE’s 2017 recommendations place fludrocortisone after midodrine when it is contraindicated, intolerable or ineffective and emphasize cardiac risk; the 2020 review additionally highlights hypokalemia monitoring and contraindications in heart or kidney failure. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

Non-drug orthostatic measures include standing slowly, avoiding heat and large carbohydrate-rich meals, and individualized water and salt intake. Supplementation requires caution with heart, kidney or liver failure; abdominal binders have better supporting evidence than compression stockings in the cited review. (low confidence)

The 2017 NICE PD recommendations advise considering midodrine with monitoring for supine hypertension, followed by consideration of fludrocortisone when midodrine is contraindicated, ineffective or not tolerated; cardiac risks and interactions matter. The OH review also warns of heart or kidney failure and hypokalemia with fludrocortisone. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

The cited sources note that treating upright hypotension requires attention to supine and nocturnal hypertension, which can coexist and limit pressor treatment, and that blood-pressure monitoring is part of management. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

PD constipation can combine slow intestinal transit with outlet obstruction caused by impaired sphincter or puborectalis coordination; assessment should distinguish these mechanisms rather than treating every case as infrequent bowel movements alone. (medium confidence)

A randomized trial of a particular multistrain probiotic preparation reported improved bowel frequency and transit time over 8 weeks; that result supports the tested preparation and duration rather than interchangeable efficacy of all probiotic products. (low confidence)

The urogenital review recommends history, bladder diary, urinalysis and post-void residual assessment, with further testing guided by findings to identify coexisting urological disease rather than attributing all urinary symptoms to PD. (low confidence)
The cited sources note that antimuscarinic bladder treatments can worsen constipation, a trade-off relevant to urinary urgency in a person with PD who already has bowel symptoms. (medium confidence)

Mirabegron results differ by study and endpoint: PaDoMi reported improved overactive-bladder symptom scores at Weeks 4 and 8 in a Parkinsonism population, whereas MAESTRO did not achieve its primary composite symptom endpoint when mirabegron was added to behavioral modification including pelvic floor exercises. These are differing study results, rather than proof of universal benefit or no benefit. (medium confidence)

The cited sources describe assessing reversible contributors to OH and reviewing medicines that lower blood pressure, including antihypertensive and dopaminergic treatments, before escalating symptom-directed treatment. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

The cited sources state that midodrine can be considered for PD-related OH, with attention to contraindications and supine hypertension; they describe supine and home blood-pressure monitoring as helping to balance upright benefit against hypertension while lying down. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

The 2019 MDS review rated droxidopa efficacious only in the short term and possibly useful, while rating the PD-specific efficacy evidence for midodrine and fludrocortisone insufficient; prescribing recommendations should not be mistaken for strong long-term PD trial evidence. (low confidence)
Macrogol has placebo-controlled evidence for PD constipation and was rated likely efficacious and possibly useful in the 2019 MDS review. (medium confidence)

In the placebo-controlled lubiprostone trial, short-term constipation improvement favored active treatment, while intermittent loose stools were the most common reported adverse event. These findings do not establish long-term comparative effectiveness. (medium confidence)

The 2019 MDS review called probiotics with prebiotic fiber efficacious and clinically useful on the basis of one trial; the 2022 meta-analysis instead concluded that evidence remained insufficient, noting few trials, heterogeneous preparations and high heterogeneity. These are attributed assessments with different evidence sets, not an unconditional endorsement of probiotics. (medium confidence)

Mirabegron bladder-trial findings differ: PaDoMi reported improved OAB symptom scores and another placebo-controlled PD trial reported positive primary outcomes, whereas MAESTRO found no significant primary composite-score benefit from adding mirabegron to behavioral modification. Results should be interpreted by population, comparator and endpoint. (medium confidence)
For refractory detrusor overactivity, the urogenital review describes intradetrusor botulinum toxin as an option but explicitly warns about urinary retention. (low confidence)

The cited sources state that orthostatic hypotension in PD should prompt review of blood-pressure-lowering medicines and correction of reversible contributors such as dehydration, and that it should not automatically be attributed solely to neurodegeneration. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

Macrogol and lubiprostone have supportive PD constipation trial evidence, but this should be described with the limits of small, short studies. The 2019 MDS review classified both as likely efficacious and possibly useful; the 2018 constipation review cautioned against strong recommendations from the evidence then available. (medium confidence)

Antimuscarinic treatment for overactive bladder in PD requires attention to worsening constipation and cognitive adverse effects; the MAESTRO investigators describe these as reasons to study alternatives. (low confidence)

Bladder treatment evidence includes important selection and safety limits: MAESTRO excluded patients with excessive post-void residual and evidence of urinary tract infection; PaDoMi reported a mild rise in residual urine and one episode of acute urinary retention. (medium confidence)

narrative.documentConcept: PD autonomic dysfunction: orthostatic hypotension, constipation, bladder
narrative.text: This section covers Parkinson’s autonomic symptoms: orthostatic hypotension, constipation and bladder symptoms. OH management combines medication review and nonpharmacological measures with selected drugs while monitoring supine hypertension. Constipation can involve slow transit and impaired evacuation; macrogol and lubiprostone have trial support. The cited review describes bladder assessment as checking coexisting urological disease and medication trade-offs. Antimuscarinics may worsen constipation, while mirabegron trials have differing outcomes. Probiotic recommendations also differ across evidence reviews; product-specific and short-term results should retain their qualifications.
